Activity
ak-TIV-i-ty
n.
From Latin activus (active), through French activite; appearing once in the Authorized Version in the idiom 'men of activity,' meaning men of capable, energetic ability.

Biblical Definition

If thou knowest any men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle.

Activity appears once in the Authorized Version, in Pharaoh's instruction to Joseph concerning the settlement of Jacob's household in Goshen. The idiom men of activity does not mean busy men in the modern sense of constant motion, but capable, energetic, competent men — those fit to be entrusted with real responsibility. Pharaoh, having already granted the best of the land to Joseph's family, goes further and invites Joseph to identify from among his brothers any men of activity suitable to be made rulers over the royal cattle, a position of genuine trust in an economy where livestock represented substantial wealth. The verse is a small but telling detail in the larger narrative of Joseph's rise: the favour shown to one faithful man extends outward to create opportunity for his whole family, and it is Joseph himself, once a slave and prisoner, who is now positioned to identify and commend competence in others. Activity here names the kind of demonstrated ability that earns trust, not mere busyness.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from ACTIVE: nimble; quick; having the power of quick motion or of ready service; here as a noun, activity, denoting capable, energetic fitness for responsibility.

ACTIVITY, n. The quality of being active; nimbleness; agility.

ACTIVITY, n. Vigorous action; energy applied to a purpose.

In the idiom 'men of activity,' capable and energetic ability suited to real responsibility.

In Genesis 47:6 the word names the qualification Pharaoh seeks in men to be set over his cattle.

The idiom contrasts with mere busyness: activity here is demonstrated fitness for trust.

Key Scripture

Gen 47:6 — "The land of Egypt is before thee; in the best of the land make thy father and brethren to dwell; in the land of Goshen let them dwell: and if thou knowest any men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle."

Modern Corruption

There is no live postmodern redefinition of this word; the entry exists because the idiom 'men of activity' names a biblical standard for entrusted responsibility — demonstrated competence — that remains as relevant to any question of who should be given charge over what as it was to Pharaoh's cattle.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Activity retains a recognizable sense across the centuries, though the specific idiom 'men of activity' has faded from common speech in favour of words like 'capable' or 'competent.'

The principle to recover is the narrative's own quiet lesson: favour shown to Joseph becomes opportunity extended to his brothers, but the standard by which they are to be advanced is not family connection alone but demonstrated activity — real fitness for the responsibility offered. Trust in Scripture is repeatedly tied to competence proven, not merely position inherited.
